body:
FIIs and prop firms are not smarter readers of the same books. They are built differently, and in Indian F&O the difference decides the outcome. SEBI's August 2026 study of FY25–FY26 found individuals lost **₹97,882 crore gross in FY25 and ₹72,243 crore in FY26**. In the same years prop traders made ₹45,955 crore and ₹44,483 crore, and FPIs ₹31,085 crore and ₹13,896 crore. **99% of FPI and prop gross profit went to entities using algorithms**, and the **top 10 prop entities took about 75% of the prop category's profit**. Options produced 92% of individual losses and about 98% of prop profit. In FY25, 70% of index-options turnover happened on expiry day ([SEBI, Aug 2026](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/aug-2026/1787233506209.pdf)). Individuals also paid about **₹25,000 crore a year in transaction costs**, roughly ₹1 lakh crore over FY22–FY26, which is a certain loss before any skill enters ([SEBI, Aug 2026](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/aug-2026/1787233506209.pdf)). The losses fall on the most fragile traders. In FY26, 43% of traders were under 30 and 89% of them lost money. **The 13% of traders with portfolios under ₹1 lakh but turnover above ₹1 crore accounted for 52% of all losses** ([SEBI, Aug 2026](https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/aug-2026/1787233506209.pdf)).

The professional business model has four parts. Firms collect the bid-ask spread on enormous volume. They sell short-dated options that retail buys, earning the premium of implied over realised volatility and the "lottery premium" on far out-of-the-money strikes. They arbitrage the index against its constituents and futures against options. And they win speed races. On London Stock Exchange data, latency races occur about once a minute per FTSE 100 stock and last 5–10 microseconds. The top six firms win or lose more than 80% of them ([FCA Occasional Paper 50](https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/occasional-papers/occasional-paper-no-50-quantifying-high-frequency-trading-arms-race-new-methodology)). The scale is enormous. Jane Street posted **$39.6 billion of net trading revenue in 2025**, more than JPMorgan's trading unit ([Hedgeweek](https://www.hedgeweek.com/jane-street-outpaces-rivals-with-record-40bn-trading-haul/)). Citadel Securities' India arm earned about ₹4,060 crore of revenue in the year to March 2025 with a team of about ten ([Samosa Capital](https://samosacapital.beehiiv.com/p/citadel-s-india-profits-surge-even-as-regulators-rein-in-trading-daily-india-briefing)). India accounts for about 60% of global equity-derivatives contract volume ([FIA](https://www.fia.org/marketvoice/articles/explainer-meteoric-rise-indias-equity-derivatives-volume)). Global trading firms are not opening offices in Mumbai for the fundamentals.

`case_study:ge-2017-2018` | 2018-10-30 | tickers: US-GE | confidence: verified

General Electric traded ~$30-32 in mid-2016 and fell to ~$6.7 by Dec 2018 (-58% in 2018 alone, worst year in >50 years; pre-2021 1:8 reverse split). Sequence: Nov 2017 dividend halved; Jan 2018 a $6.2 bn after-tax charge on run-off long-term-care insurance plus ~$15 bn of statutory reserve contributions over 7 years; Oct 2018 a $22 bn goodwill impairment in GE Power (largely Alstom, bought 2015) and dividend cut to $0.01; SEC/DOJ probes; 2019 Markopolos report alleged further LTC under-reserving (GE disputed). Recovery came only after Larry Culp's deleveraging and the break-up into GE Aerospace, GE Vernova and GE HealthCare (2023-24). Visible flags: (1) industrial CFO flattered by selling receivables to GE Capital ('factoring') and 'deferred monetisation' of service contracts (contract assets growing faster than revenue); (2) dividend exceeding free cash flow; (3) a long-tail insurance liability inside an industrial company; (4) Alstom paid at the power cycle peak -> goodwill; (5) consistent 'beat by a penny' earnings and heavy non-GAAP adjustments; (6) repeated CEO changes in 2017-18. Lesson: a low P/E on 'normal' earnings is a trap when earnings quality is low; check contract assets, receivable sales and dividend cover by FCF. Index weight and history are not safety.

**Lesson:** Low P/E on poor-quality earnings is a value trap
**Spotted early by:** JPMorgan's Steve Tusa (sell from 2017); Markopolos (2019, contested)
**Links:** illustrates -> `insight:value-trap-patterns`, illustrates -> `insight:forensic-redflag-checklist`

`event:india-demonetisation-2016` | confidence: **verified** | tags: india, policy, smallcap, sector-realty, sector-nbfc

On 8 Nov 2016 Rs 500/1,000 notes (~86% of currency by value) were withdrawn. Nifty: above 8,500 before the move (8 Nov close cited ~8,516-8,544) to a seven-month low of 7,908 on 26 Dec 2016, about -7%. Hardest hit: BSE Realty -17% (8 Nov - 26 Dec); microfinance and gold-loan NBFCs such as Bharat Financial Inclusion and Manappuram fell 40%+; consumer discretionary and cash-heavy sectors. By mid-Feb 2017 benchmarks were ~3% above their 8 Nov close; Bharat Financial and Manappuram had rallied ~60% from December lows - helped by a stemming of FPI outflows, a better-than-feared December-quarter, and strong domestic MF buying. 2017 then became a broad small-cap and realty rally: Nifty Realty +~97% (biggest in a decade), with small caps also surging (BSE Smallcap ~+60% in 2017, from memory). Analysts noted demonetisation plus GST deferred earnings recovery by ~3 quarters. Signal: the shock was a liquidity/sentiment hit, not a balance-sheet crisis, and domestic flows (SIPs, post-demonetisation 'financialisation of savings') were rising. Lesson: policy shocks that don't damage the banking system are usually bought within months; but the flood of domestic money that followed fed the 2017 small-cap froth that crashed in 2018.

| key | value |
|---|---|
| nifty | ~8,516-8,544 -> 7,908 (26 Dec 2016) |
| drawdown | ~-7% |
| realty | -17% then +97% in 2017 |
| nbfc_mfi | -40% then +60% by Feb 2017 |
| lesson | non-systemic policy shocks are bought fast |

body:
**What it means.**
1. **Promises that ride the cycle are now reliable, and conservative.** FY26 was guided mid-teens and came in at +21.4%. Every quarter-on-quarter guide from Q4 FY25 to Q2 FY27 was met or beaten. FY27 has been raised three times: mid-teens (Feb-26), "in line with FY26" (May-26), "couple of points above" (Aug-26), and **+24%** (Nov-26). H1 FY27 is running at +32%.
2. **Execution promises slip, and each slip is described as "on track".** Mexico was due to start in January 2026. The first dispatch went out in November 2026, about 10 months late, after four restated dates that were each called on schedule. The USD 9–10m CY26 base case quietly became "single-digit USD m in H2 FY27".
3. **The acquisition was a two-year narrative with no deal.** In Aug-24 it was coming "soon". In Nov-24 it was due "within the next year or so". In Feb-25 it was meant to supply 25–30% of sales. On 2026-05-26 management finally admitted it, when asked: about 12 targets screened and 2 near-misses that both fell through. The "third platform" is now organic fabrication, at under 2% of revenue today, aiming for 8–10% in 18–24 months. The October 2025 special dividend of ₹101.6 cr was the honest result of that admission.
4. **Aftermarket is the clearest case of goalposts moving.** In FY25 it was guided at +25–30% (Nov-24, and again in Feb-25, 7 weeks before year-end) and delivered +20%. For FY26 it was guided at "mid-teens" (Aug-25), then "single digit" (Nov-25, with the COO saying "we definitely have not de-grown"), then called a "stable contributor". The actual figure was **about −9%**: 20% of ₹964 cr fell to 15% of ₹1,170 cr, per the CEO's own shares given in Aug-26. In Q2 FY27 it rebounded more than 50% YoY, which met the Aug-26 promise that it would "normalise in 12 months".
5. **Candour is low.** Explanations for misses (tariffs, IMMEX registration, customer destocking, deals falling apart) are reasonable, but almost all came out only when an analyst pushed. The worst example is Feb-25. Asked whether Q4 FY25 would be the highest quarter, the promoter said "somebody asked me, is it going to be the highest? I said no", although he had said exactly that on the Aug-24 and Nov-24 calls. In Aug-24 an analyst said the calls sounded like *"Tarikh pe tarikh"* (date after date). The Q4 FY24 call adds the pre-history: FY25 had been guided at mid-teens growth in Feb-24, was "being reassessed" by May-24, cut to flat/−3% in Aug-24, and landed at −15%.

- **2026-11-21 D1 (clarification, before any statistic).** The period label is set from the event date and the fiscal
  quarter together. An event dated 2026 whose fiscal quarter is *not* one of the four fresh quarters (a late filer for
  Sep-2025 or earlier) belongs to neither period and is counted in `counts.other`. Re-run = events dated 2022–2025.
- **D2 (clarification, before any statistic).** H4 tertile drift is computed as in v1. Events are split by mcap tertile
  within each fiscal quarter, then ranked into SUE quintiles within each (quarter, tertile) cell of ≥ 15 events. The
  H4 rows show top-vs-controls and T−B per tertile.
- **D3 (operational).** Pass A ran as two processes on two halves of the ordered list (each with its own rate gaps:
  API 1.0 s, archive 0.3 s, Yahoo 1.1 s), and the all-company announcements feed ran alongside at 1.5 s/call. A smoke
  test of the event and analysis code ran on partial pass-A data with all output discarded. Only structural counts
  were looked at (events per quarter and EPS basis, event-date source), never a return.
